title: Personality and Roots of Welfare State Support: How Openness to Experience Moderates the Influence of Self-Interest and Ideology on Redistributive Preferences

selected_claim.evidence_location: Table 3, Model 4, and the “Self-Interested Evaluations of Redistributive Policies” section; the interpretation is also shown in Fig. 2.
selected_claim.evidence_summary: In individual fixed-effects models using waves 2–3, the estimated association between logged personal income and support for redistribution is negative and statistically significant among the low-openness (close-minded) reference group (income coefficient −0.16, p < 0.01). The income associations for medium- and high-openness groups are attenuated by the interaction terms. This is an adjusted observational estimate based on within-person changes, not a randomized or difference-in-differences estimate.
selected_claim.x: Respondents’ personal gross income, measured from registry data, natural-log transformed; the fixed-effects estimate uses within-person income changes.
selected_claim.y: Respondents’ support for redistribution, measured by agreement with “The government should take measures to reduce differences in income levels,” rescaled from 0 to 1 with higher values indicating stronger support.
selected_claim.target_population: Danish Social and Political Attitudes Panel Survey respondents with observations in waves 2 and 3 included in the fixed-effects analysis (Table 3, Model 4; 969 observations), with the reported income association for the low-openness group.
selected_claim.adjustment_description: Table 3, Model 4 adjusts for years of education, social-benefit receipt, and the other Big Five personality traits; it also includes individual and wave fixed effects. Openness is categorized, with medium- and high-openness indicators and their interactions with income, so the income coefficient represents the low-openness reference group.
covariates: Categorical openness (medium and high openness indicators; openness is the moderator)

evidence_summary: The focal paper estimates the association of within-person changes in personal gross income with support for redistribution among respondents in the low-openness reference group. Income is registry-measured and natural-log transformed; the outcome is agreement that government should reduce income differences, rescaled 0–1. Table 3 Model 4 includes individual and wave fixed effects and adjusts for education, social-benefit receipt, and other Big Five traits; medium- and high-openness indicators and income interactions are included.

category-financial-behavior.reason: The income-side findings concern several distinct behaviors—investment and trading, borrowing, microenterprise investment, domestic-service purchases, and family income pooling. The outcome-side findings concern investment or share-holding behavior linked to market or reform attitudes. Investment behavior is the meaningful overlap; the broader set of behaviors does not support one common confounder inference across both links.
category-financial-behavior.exposure_examples: For the income link, examples include investment activity, mutual-fund and asset-class investment timing, trading, microenterprise investment, microcredit borrowing, outsourcing domestic services, and family income pooling. These do not all represent the same financial action.
category-financial-behavior.outcome_examples: For the outcome link, examples include investing in stocks linked to distrust of financial markets and retaining voucher-privatization shares linked to support for economic reform or markets.
category-financial-behavior.why_not_confounder: The broad category combines behaviors with different mechanisms. Evidence that investment or share-holding relates to economic attitudes cannot establish that borrowing, purchasing domestic services, or pooling household income has the same relationship to those attitudes; nor can the income-side links alone establish a shared confounder across the broad category.
category-financial-behavior.new_group_rationale: A narrower group of financial investment behavior is coherent across the relevant examples: stock investment or share retention can relate to economic attitudes, while investment and trading activity can relate to accrued returns or earnings.
category-financial-behavior.residual_group_rationale: The residual group, other financial behavior, remains coherent as actual allocation or movement of money that is not investment behavior, including borrowing, household pooling, and purchasing domestic services. Its income-side links do not, by themselves, support a common link to economic attitudes.
category-financial-behavior.boundary_cases: Investment-related borrowing or microenterprise investment may fit either investment behavior or borrowing, depending on whether the behavior being studied is the loan transaction or the deployment of the loan. Household income pooling and purchases of domestic services belong in the residual group. The evidence is limited for whether any residual behavior also shapes redistribution preferences.

category-prosocial-orientation-charitabl.reason: The income-side findings concern participation in, duration of, or experience from volunteering and link that behavior to wages. The outcome-side findings concern prosocial preferences or compassion and link those dispositions to redistribution support. The former may operate through labor-market experience or signaling, while the latter may operate through concern for others; the evidence does not establish that these are one common confounder.
category-prosocial-orientation-charitabl.exposure_examples: Volunteering participation among Italian workers; duration of volunteering in German panel data; years of volunteer-work experience among labor-market entrants and established workers; volunteering hours or participation associated with wage rates.
category-prosocial-orientation-charitabl.outcome_examples: General prosocial preferences predicting support for income redistribution in a New Zealand sample; compassion for others associated with support for wealth redistribution among British people.
category-prosocial-orientation-charitabl.why_not_confounder: The two links do not jointly establish one common prosocial cause of both income and redistribution preferences. The income evidence concerns volunteer activity or experience with possible labor-market returns; the outcome evidence concerns prosocial dispositions or compassion. Volunteer activity may reflect a prosocial disposition, but the findings do not show that the same disposition explains the wage associations.
category-prosocial-orientation-charitabl.new_group_rationale: A group for volunteering and charitable behavior would coherently cover participation, hours, duration, and accumulated volunteer-work experience that may relate to earnings through experience, skills, or signaling.
category-prosocial-orientation-charitabl.residual_group_rationale: A residual group for prosocial preferences and altruistic concern would coherently cover general prosocial preferences and compassion as dispositions that may shape support for redistribution.
category-prosocial-orientation-charitabl.boundary_cases: Volunteering may be motivated by altruism, career development, or both, and volunteer experience can build skills as well as signal them. It is uncertain whether such behavior is a reliable measure of stable prosocial orientation. General prosocial preferences and compassion also may overlap, but neither is equivalent to observed volunteering. The split separates the measured concepts and proposed links without ruling out overlap.

Individual fixed effects (c7) absorb stable between-person differences, including enduring race, ethnicity, and national or immigrant origin. This is a design feature, not a direct measured control. It does not absorb changes in income or other time-varying conditions, nor any change in identity or origin-related circumstances within a person; the confounder here is defined as a relatively stable background characteristic.

Individual fixed effects (c7) absorb stable between-person differences in religious affiliation and other stable religious orientations. This is a design feature, not a direct control. It does not absorb within-person changes in religiosity, belief, or religious practice; the wave fixed effects address only period changes common across respondents.

Individual fixed effects (c7) absorb stable between-person variation in sexuality or gender identity, so stable identity differences cannot explain the within-person income association. This is a design feature, not a direct control. It does not absorb changes in identity or expression, or time-varying effects of identity-related circumstances.

Individual fixed effects (c7) absorb stable between-person differences in social interaction, such as enduring network participation or relationship patterns. They do not absorb time-varying changes in contact, relationships, support, or social participation across waves, so this is only partial adjustment.
